objectives: Define the Ahî Organization and its historical role.
Explain the possible origins of the word ‘Ahî’.
Explain why the fütüvvet tradition must be studied first.
Use non-defining relative clauses, be derived from, subsequently and participle phrases.
content.pedagogy: A dense academic opening that defines the institution, explains its name and sets up the next chapter. Learners practice unpacking compact noun phrases and participle phrases.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The book gives two possible origins of the word; it does not choose one.
‘Ahî’ in the Arabic reading means ‘my brother’, while ‘ah’ means ‘brother’.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: non-defining relative clauses (which) · be derived from · subsequently · participle phrases (meaning …) · to + verb (purpose)
Notice (Activity 1): meaning ‘brother’.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *, that emerged · *is derived of · *subsequently (= as a result).
Use (Activity 4): define an institution.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: a-HÎ, fü-tüv-VET.
Stress: sub-SE-quent-ly, so-ci-o-CUL-tur-al, com-MER-cial, de-RIVED.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do historians often study where a word comes from?”
duringReading: First reading: What was the Ahî Organization?
Second reading: complete a chart of the two origins.
Find why fütüvvet comes next.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Origins chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: define an institution; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What areas of life did the institution guide?
Why might the idea of brotherhood be important for this institution?
Why does the writer begin the next chapter with fütüvvet?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “13th-Century Anatolia” and “‘Ahî’: My Brother” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: emerged, subsequently, commercial life, derived, grasp, function, principles, establishment.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the two words written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short encyclopedia entry for the Ahî Organization using two participle phrases.

formativeAssessment: Explains both origins of the word.
expectedResponses: The Ahî Organization, which emerged in 13th-century Anatolia, was a religious and social institution that later helped establish the Ottoman Empire. Its name is derived either from the Arabic ‘ah’, meaning ‘brother’, or from the Turkish ‘akı’, meaning ‘generous and brave’.
content.transferTask: Define an institution in your country.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners unpack the participle phrases?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “be derived from” and one with a participle phrase.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses be derived from and a participle.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners give a one-minute overview of the Ahî Organization, including both possible origins of its name. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads up to “commercial life” and B reads the rest. Each summarizes the part in two sentences and the partner asks a follow-up question about it.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentences on the word “Ahî”. Asker asks “Why does the Arabic reading mean ‘my brother’?” Explainer explains the role of the final “î”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A foreign student at a cultural fair asks what “Ahî” means. The learner explains both readings and says why the meaning “brother” fits the organization.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Throughout the centuries, the institution guided society with principles and rules governing moral, sociocultural, and commercial life.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the Ahî Organization was and why its name is linked to brotherhood. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter ends by sending the reader back to fütüvvet. Why might a writer start with a definition and then go back in time?” (To show that the Ahîs grew out of an older tradition.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners present both etymologies without claiming one is certain. They use “is derived from” accurately.

thinkAloud.sentence: The Ahî Organization, which emerged in 13th-century Anatolia, was a religious and social institution that subsequently played a crucial role in the establishment of the Ottoman Empire.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The main clause is “The Ahî Organization was a religious and social institution”. The “which” clause adds when and where, and the “that” clause adds its later role. I read the core first and then the extra information. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “The word ‘Ahî’ is derived either from the Arabic word ‘ah’, meaning ‘brother’, or from the Turkish word ‘akı’, meaning ‘generous and brave’.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What are the two possible origins of the word “Ahî”?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences: Which institution in your town today guides people’s moral and working life?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one similarity or difference to the Ahî Organization.

objectives: Trace the development of fütüvvet through its stages.
Explain what changed and what stayed the same.
Explain how fütüvvet became the Ahî movement in Anatolia.
Use participle clauses, as for time and from … onwards.
content.pedagogy: The chapter traces the evolution of a concept over six centuries. A time line with five stages, and a column for “what stayed the same”, helps learners see both change and continuity.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The term ‘fetâ’ comes from the pre-Islamic period; fütüvvet emerged in the first century of Islam.
In its final stage, fütüvvet kept most of its Sufi character; it did not lose it completely.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: participle clauses (rooted in …; functioning as …) · as (= while) · while + -ing · from … onwards · refer to / adopt / acquire
Notice (Activity 1): functioning as … while mostly keeping …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *rooting in · *From the 13th century ago · *referred qualities.
Use (Activity 4): the evolution of an idea.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: fü-tüv-VET, fe-TÂ, ab-BA-sid.
Stress: FEAR-less-ness, HELP-ful-ness, IN-te-grat-ed, ON-wards.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can you think of a tradition that changed over time but kept its spirit?”
duringReading: First reading: Where did fütüvvet begin?
Second reading: make a time line of five stages.
Find what fütüvvet kept in its final stage.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Time line; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: the evolution of an idea; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What qualities did ‘fetâ’ refer to?
How did the Sufi movement change fütüvvet?
Why is it important that fütüvvet kept its Sufi character?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Fetâ” and “The Abbasids” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: virtue, expanded from, adopted, onwards, acquired, politically, integrated.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the time line with the periods written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph comparing the first and the final stage of fütüvvet.

expectedResponses: Fütüvvet, rooted in the pre-Islamic term ‘fetâ’, emerged in the first century of Islam. It became a youth movement, adopted a Sufi identity, became an official organization under the Abbasids and finally joined the artisan class, while keeping most of its Sufi character. It reached Anatolia and became the Ahî movement.
content.transferTask: Trace how an idea or tradition evolved.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see both change and continuity?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “rooted in” and one with “From … onwards”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners summarize how fütüvvet developed from a concept into a professional organization. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner the difference between fütüvvet as a concept and fütüvvet as an organization. The partner gives one example from the text for each.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about the final stage. Asker asks “What did fütüvvet keep?” Explainer paraphrases “mostly keeping its Sufi character”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: In a history podcast, the host asks, “How did a word become a movement?” The learner answers in four steps.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The concept of fütüvvet reached Anatolia through the Abbasids.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how fütüvvet changed over several centuries before it reached Anatolia. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Which verbs show change in this chapter, and why does the writer use so many?” (Developed into, expanded, adopted, became, became integrated, turned into: the chapter is about a process.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the stages in order, with at least three verbs of change.

thinkAloud.sentence: In its final stage, it became integrated with the artisan class, functioning as a professional organization while mostly keeping its Sufi character.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “In its final stage” tells me this is the end of the process. The participle “functioning” explains how it worked, and “while” adds what stayed the same. So there is both change and continuity here. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “By the 9th century, the concept developed into a structured movement organizing young people socially, economically, and politically.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: In which three ways did the movement organize young people?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences: Which quality of “fetâ” do you think is most needed today, and why?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with a different quality and a reason.

objectives: Explain the Caliph’s political aims.
Describe Sühreverdî’s role.
Explain the meaning of the robe ceremony in Konya.
Use participle clauses of reason, by + -ing, consequently, upon and would for future in the past.
content.pedagogy: A political chapter with dense B2 language: participle clauses, formal linkers and future in the past. A chain (aim → envoy → plan → ceremony → recognition) makes the argument visible.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Caliph regarded himself as the leader of the fütüvvet order; he did not join a Seljuk order.
The robe ceremony meant that the Caliph recognized the Sultan’s authority, not the opposite.
“Envoy” and “emissary” refer to the same person here.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: participle clauses of reason (Being …) · by + -ing · consequently · would be + past participle (future in the past) · upon + noun · not just … but also
Notice (Activity 1): Being a well-known mufassir …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Consequently (= but) · *will be brought (past context) · *Upon he arrived.
Use (Activity 4): a symbolic act.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: â-lâ-ed-DİN key-ku-BAD, nâ-SIR li-dî-nil-LÂH, es-süh-re-ver-DÎ.
Stress: EM-is-sar-y, EN-voy, le-GIT-i-ma-cy, cer-e-MO-ni-al.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do rulers send gifts to each other? What can a gift mean?”
duringReading: First reading: What did the Caliph send, and why?
Second reading: make the chain aim → envoy → plan → ceremony → recognition.
Find what the ceremony meant.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Chain; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a symbolic act; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the Caliph choose Sühreverdî?
What would change for the fütüvvet groups?
What did the ceremony in Konya mean for both rulers?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Fütüvvet Robe” and “Konya” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: emissary, envoy, scattered, grant, legitimacy, carrying out, immense, ceremonial, robe, recognized.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chain with the first and last boxes filled.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short analysis of the ceremony from the Caliph’s point of view.

formativeAssessment: Uses a participle clause or consequently correctly.
expectedResponses: The Caliph, who saw himself as leader of the fütüvvet order, wanted to give fütüvvet official status and bring it under state control. Being a respected scholar and Sufi, Sühreverdî could unite the groups. In Konya, he dressed Keykubad in the ceremonial robe, and the Caliph thus recognized Keykubad’s authority.
content.transferTask: Write about a symbolic act in history or in your community.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners follow the political argument?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “Being …, …” and one with “Consequently, …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses a participle clause or consequently.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain the political purpose behind the robe sent to Alâeddin Keykubad I. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraph 2. Each explains the aim of the Caliph from his or her paragraph. Together they write one sentence that joins both aims.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence with “Consequently”. Asker asks “What was the result for the institution?” Explainer explains “brought under state control”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A museum guide in Konya presents a copy of the robe to visitors and explains in one minute why it mattered.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Through this act, the Abbasid Caliph officially recognized Keykubad’s political authority.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why the Caliph sent a robe to the sultan and what this act meant for both of them. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Who gained what from this ceremony?” (The Caliph gained support and control; Keykubad gained recognition of his authority.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain both sides of the exchange and use “legitimacy” or “recognized” correctly.

thinkAloud.sentence: By transforming the organization into a governmental body, he sought to give it legitimacy and secure its political support.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “By … -ing” shows the method and “sought to” shows the aim. The method is making it a governmental body. The aims are legitimacy and political support. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “The envoy sent by the caliph was Şehâbeddin es-Sühreverdî (d. 1234).”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Why did Sühreverdî have enough influence for this task?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences: Why do leaders use symbols such as robes, flags or medals?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one example from your country.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: Ahî Evran and the Spread of the Ahîs
objectives: Describe Ahî Evran and the spread of the Ahî order.
Explain how the Ahîs gained political and military power.
Describe the Ahîs’ role against Gıyâseddin II and the Mongols.
Use participle clauses of reason, the perfect passive infinitive, the past perfect and a period when.
content.pedagogy: A chapter that links an individual (Ahî Evran) with a social movement and with political crisis. A map of Ahî Evran’s journey and a time line of events (Keykubad I → Gıyâseddin II → Kösedağ → Tokat, Sivas → Kayseri) support comprehension.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The poisoning is presented as a belief (“is believed to have been”), not as a proven fact.
The Mongols had already seized Tokat and Sivas before the defense of Kayseri.
Kayseri eventually fell; the defense did not save it.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: participle clauses of reason (suspecting …) · is believed to have been + past participle · past perfect (had already seized) · a period when · although
Notice (Activity 1): is believed to have been poisoned.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *is believed to be poisoned (past) · *have already seized (past context) · *a period which.
Use (Activity 4): when authority breaks down.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: a-HÎ ev-RAN, kır-şe-HİR, kö-se-DAĞ, to-KAT, SI-vas.
Stress: as-sas-si-NA-tion, se-mi-no-MAD-ic, AN-ar-chy, ad-min-is-TRA-tions.
beforeReading: Ask: “What happens to a city when the government cannot protect it?”
duringReading: First reading: Who was Ahî Evran?
Second reading: draw his route and mark the political events on a time line.
Find what the Ahîs did during the Mongol invasion.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Map and time line; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: when authority breaks down; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the Ahî order spread so quickly?
Why did the Ahîs become powerful when state authority was weak?
How does the writer show uncertainty about the poisoning?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Kırşehir” and “Kösedağ” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: tanners, artisans, dwellers, nomadic, semi-nomadic, demonstrated, assassination, faithfully, poisoned, defense, seized, eventually.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the map with the cities marked and the time line partly filled.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short biography of Ahî Evran with a participle clause and a past perfect.

formativeAssessment: Describes Ahî Evran and the spread of the order.
Explains the Ahîs’ power in a crisis.
Uses the perfect passive infinitive or a participle clause correctly.
expectedResponses: Ahî Evran, a Sufi scholar from Central Asia, settled in Kırşehir and made it a center for artisans. When state authority was weak, the Ahîs took control of city administrations. They resisted Gıyâseddin II, suspecting him of Keykubad I’s death, and defended Kayseri against the Mongols, although the city eventually fell.
content.transferTask: Write about how a community organizes itself in a crisis.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice the writer’s caution about the poisoning?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “is believed to have been …” and one with a participle clause of reason.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes Ahî Evran and the order.
Uses a B2 structure from the chapter.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain how the Ahîs gained political power in 13th-century Anatolia. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 2 and B reads paragraph 3. Each summarizes his or her paragraph in two sentences. The partner asks how the two paragraphs are linked.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about Ahî Evran’s titles. Asker asks “Which three titles does he have?” Explainer explains “versatile scholar”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor in Kırşehir asks why the city is linked to craftsmen. The learner answers using Ahî Evran’s story.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The members of this organization spread rapidly throughout Anatolia.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, who Ahî Evran was and what the Ahîs did when state authority collapsed. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why did the Ahîs resist Gıyâseddin II?” (They suspected him of the assassination of his father, who had supported them.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners link weak central authority with the Ahîs’ urban role and use “during times when” or “a period when”.

thinkAloud.sentence: They demonstrated their political and military power during times when central authority broke down and anarchy emerged.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “During times when” gives me the context. The Ahîs filled a gap left by the state. The next sentence about the Mongol invasion is an example of this. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Known as the spiritual leader of tanners and other craftsmen, Ahî Evran established a zaviye in Kırşehir that became the socio-religious and professional center for artisans all across Anatolia.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What did the zaviye in Kırşehir become?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences: What do local groups do in your town when there is a crisis?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question about his or her example.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Values and Way of Life
objectives: Explain the economic role of the Ahî order.
Explain the role of the Fütüvvetnameler.
Summarize the key characteristics of the Fütüvvet way of life.
Use participle phrases, be expected to, it is crucial to, while + -ing and furthermore.
content.pedagogy: The chapter connects economic regulation (quality, prices, relations with the state) with personal ethics (honesty, kindness, generosity). The connection between business and morality is a strong discussion topic for B2.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The order functioned like trade guilds; it was not a government ministry.
The Fütüvvetnameler were handbooks of the organization, not legal codes of the state.
“Company” here means the people you spend time with, not a business.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: opening past participle phrases (Rooted in …) · be expected to · while + -ing · it is crucial to · furthermore · finally
Notice (Activity 1): Rooted in Islamic-Sufi thought …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Rooting in … · *expected being · *crucial avoiding.
Use (Activity 4): a code of conduct.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: fü-tüv-vet-na-me-LER, tek-KE, zâ-vi-YE, a-le-vi bek-TA-shi.
Stress: JOUR-ney-men, en-FORC-ing, REG-u-lat-ing, char-ac-ter-IS-tics.
beforeReading: Ask: “Should a good businessperson also be a good person? Why?”
duringReading: First reading: What was the order responsible for?
Second reading: complete the chart: economy / ethics.
Find where the values were recorded.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Economy / ethics chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a code of conduct; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why would an organization regulate prices and quality?
How are economic rules and ethical rules connected in this chapter?
Which characteristic of the Fütüvvet way of life is most relevant today?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Trade Guilds” and “Fütüvvetnameler” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: tekkes, zaviyes, regulating, guide, treat workers well, share meals, company, seek the company of wise elders, fellow, exchanging gifts.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with one item in each column.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph comparing the Ahî code with a modern business code.

formativeAssessment: Uses a participle phrase or it is crucial to correctly.
expectedResponses: Rooted in Islamic-Sufi thought, the Ahî order regulated relations in workshops, resolved trade issues and enforced quality and prices. Its values, recorded in the Fütüvvetnameler, expected followers to be generous, honest and grateful, to treat workers well and to avoid bad company.
content.transferTask: Write a code of conduct for a modern profession.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect economy and ethics?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “Rooted in …” and one with “It is crucial to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses a B2 structure from the chapter.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners summarize the Fütüvvet way of life in four rules and rank them by importance. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner explains paragraph 1 to a partner who has not read it, using “regulating” and “resolving”. The partner restates it in simpler words.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 3. Asker asks “Which rules use ‘must’?” Explainer explains why these rules are stronger.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visiting student asks about the rules of good behavior in your culture. The learner answers and compares two of them with Fütüvvet rules.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The Fütüvvet way of life includes several key characteristics that guide a person’s behavior.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the Fütüvvetnameler recorded and which Fütüvvet rules guided daily life. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The modals change from ‘are expected to’ to ‘should’ to ‘must’. What does this tell us about the rules?” (They go from general expectations to strict duties.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give four rules and use at least two modals with the right strength.

thinkAloud.sentence: Finally, followers must stay away from actions forbidden by the Qur’an and the Sunnah, such as consuming alcohol, and remember that this world is temporary.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Must” shows a strict duty, not advice. “Such as” introduces one example. I also notice a second duty after “and”: to remember that this world is temporary. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Additionally, enforcing quality control and regulating prices were among the primary duties of the order.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Which two primary duties of the order does the text name?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences: Which Fütüvvet rule would improve workplaces today?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate and say whether you agree, with a reason.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: Education in the Ahî Organization
objectives: Explain the role of role models and seeking knowledge in Ahî education.
Describe the ranks of training and the supervision of members.
Explain the role of the zaviyes as schools and cultural centers.
Use conditional rules, therefore, ultimately, under supervision and passive reporting.
content.pedagogy: The richest educational chapter of the book: role models, seeking knowledge, ranks, supervision and zaviyes as schools. It invites comparison with mentoring, internships and character education today.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Apprentices did not become masters directly; they first became journeymen.
Zaviyes were not only religious places; they functioned as schools and cultural centers.
“Promoting good and forbidding evil” is presented as a quality of role models.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: if + present, must + base verb · reduced relative clauses (skills needed for …) · therefore · ultimately · under supervision · passive (were taught through)
Notice (Activity 1): If individuals lack the skills …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *If individuals will lack · *Ultimately (= at first) · *below supervision.
Use (Activity 4): education beyond the classroom.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: zâ-vi-YE, ha-LAL.
Stress: vo-CA-tion-al, LIVE-li-hood, su-per-VI-sion, FLOUR-ished.
beforeReading: Ask: “Who teaches you more: books, teachers or the people you admire? Why?”
duringReading: First reading: What makes a good role model?
Second reading: list the ranks and the ways rules were taught.
Find what zaviyes functioned as.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Ranks and methods; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: education beyond the classroom; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why were role models so important in Ahî education?
Why did failing to learn a craft bring shame?
How were the zaviyes similar to and different from schools today?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Role Models” and “Zaviyes” when the picture is in place.

Word Notes: Role models, develop good behavior, receive vocational training, qualities, possess, attachments, tied to, promoting good, forbidding evil, seeking knowledge, fundamental requirement, seek guidance, properly, brings shame, Ultimately, ranks, advanced to, supervision, provided, functioned, flourished.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a list of qualities and ranks to tick while reading.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write an argument for or against the idea that character should be taught at school, using evidence from the chapter.

formativeAssessment: Explains the role of role models and knowledge.
Uses a conditional rule or ultimately correctly.
expectedResponses: Role models helped people develop good behavior and receive vocational training. Seeking knowledge was a fundamental requirement: if members lacked skills, they had to learn from a master. They advanced from apprentice to journeyman to master, and zaviyes functioned as schools and cultural centers.
content.transferTask: Compare Ahî education with education today.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners make thoughtful comparisons with education today?

exitTicket: Write one rule with “If …, … must …” and one conclusion with “Ultimately, …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses a conditional rule or ultimately.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain how education worked in the Ahî organization and why it mattered. The partner checks one fact in the book.

metadata.title: The Ahî Organization B2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: The Ahî Organization (Ahilik)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 8 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow extended texts about history, society and ethics, and who can produce clear, detailed explanations, evaluations and arguments.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the history of the Ahî Organization: its fütüvvet roots, its political role among the Seljuks and Ottomans, its economic and ethical rules, its education and its rituals, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. At B2, learners also notice how the writer signals certainty (It is known that / is believed to have been) and attributes views to sources, and they use these forms in their own writing.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 8 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a map, a date or a picture.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: definition, evolution, political argument, cause and result, code of conduct or interpretation.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B2 transfer: an explanation, evaluation or argument about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? How certain is the writer?), let learners formulate the rule, then confirm it and practice it in context. B2 targets include participle clauses, non-defining relative clauses, the perfect passive infinitive, future in the past, impersonal passives and formal linkers. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: non-defining relative clauses (which) · be derived from · subsequently · participle phrases (meaning …) · to + verb (purpose)
Ch2: participle clauses (rooted in …; functioning as …) · as (= while) · while + -ing · from … onwards · refer to / adopt / acquire
Ch3: participle clauses of reason (Being …) · by + -ing · consequently · would be + past participle (future in the past) · upon + noun · not just … but also
Ch4: participle clauses of reason (suspecting …) · is believed to have been + past participle · past perfect (had already seized) · a period when · although
Ch5: opening past participle phrases (Rooted in …) · be expected to · while + -ing · it is crucial to · furthermore · finally
Ch6: if + present, must + base verb · reduced relative clauses (skills needed for …) · therefore · ultimately · under supervision · passive (were taught through)
Ch7: it is known that · be known to have + past participle · not only … but also · attribute … to · mention … as · however · in conclusion
Ch8: with + noun + -ing · thus + -ing · hold (symbolic) significance · that is to say · parallel imperatives

skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify definitions, stages, political aims, degrees of certainty, attributed views and conclusions.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: explain and evaluate institutions, compare past and present, attribute views and present balanced positions.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce clear, detailed B2 paragraphs and short arguments with evidence, hedging and balanced conclusions.

languageFocus: Every one of the 8 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).

metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.
Chapter 4 says Keykubad I “is believed to have been poisoned by his son.” Present it as a belief, as the book does.
Bracketed Turkish words in the text belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

Draw a time line of the political events.

thinkAloud.sentence: Finally, followers must stay away from actions forbidden by the Qur’an and the Sunnah, such as consuming alcohol, and remember that this world is temporary.

metadata.title: The Ahî Organization B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study the history of the Ahî Organization alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 8 chapters of The Ahî Organization.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the roots, political role and decline of the Ahî Organization.
Evaluate its economic, ethical and educational legacy with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 8.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One Ahî idea that I think is still relevant today, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 8 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows honesty, hard work, helpfulness and respect. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Honesty: Honesty: Followers were expected to be honest, the order enforced quality control, and the writer separates facts from beliefs (Chapters 4, 5 and 7).
Diligence: Diligence: Seeking knowledge was a fundamental requirement, and members advanced through ranks under supervision (Chapter 6).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Followers shared meals, treated workers well, exchanged gifts and made donations (Chapter 5).
Respect: Respect: Members sought the company of wise elders and formed close ties with scholars (Chapters 5 and 6).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 8, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Explain to someone at home in six sentences what the Ahî Organization was and why it mattered, in your home language or in English.
